nameStory: The name "prickly tree-clubmoss" tells you exactly what you're looking at! It's called "tree" because it grows upright like a tiny evergreen tree, "clubmoss" because it produces spores in club-shaped structures (though it's not actually a moss), and "prickly" because its needle-like leaves give it a rougher texture than its smooth relatives.
description: Prickly tree-clubmoss is an ancient spore-producing plant that looks like a miniature evergreen forest growing on the woodland floor. These primitive plants stand 6-12 inches tall with upright branches that spread horizontally like tiny pine trees. Unlike true mosses, they have a sturdy structure with needle-like leaves densely packed around their stems. They're part of an ancient plant family that dominated forests millions of years before flowering plants evolved.

idTips.label: Round side shoots
idTips.description: Roll the horizontal branches between your fingers - they feel perfectly round and firm, like tiny green cables covered in needle-like leaves

idTips.label: Tree-like growth
idTips.description: The overall shape looks like a miniature evergreen tree with a central trunk and horizontal side branches

idTips.label: Uniform needle leaves
idTips.description: All the tiny needle-like leaves are the same size, densely packed around the stems giving it a bottle-brush texture

idTips.label: Prickly texture
idTips.description: When you gently brush your hand across it, it feels rough and prickly compared to other clubmosses

idTips.label: Evergreen appearance
idTips.description: Stays bright green year-round and maintains its shape even under snow

habitat: Look for prickly tree-clubmoss in rich, moist woodlands with well-draining sandy or humus-rich soil. It thrives in the dappled shade of mixed or coniferous forests, often growing alongside ferns and other moisture-loving plants. You'll find it scattered across the forest floor in northern New England's cooler regions, especially in areas that stay consistently moist but never waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears bright green as the plant emerges from melting snow. This is when the contrast between old and new growth is most visible.
seasonality.summer: The plant reaches its fullest, most lush appearance with dense green foliage. All identifying features are at their most prominent.
seasonality.fall: Remains bright green while surrounding plants change color, making it easy to spot against fallen leaves. May produce spore-bearing structures.
seasonality.winter: Stays evergreen under snow cover, often one of the few green things visible in the winter forest. The sturdy structure holds up well to snow weight.

funFact: This "living fossil" has been essentially unchanged for over 400 million years - meaning the prickly tree-clubmoss you see today looked exactly the same when the first fish were crawling onto land, long before dinosaurs, flowers, or even trees as we know them existed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with flat-branched tree-clubmoss, but remember: "round and rough" for prickly (this species) versus "flat and smooth" for flat-branched. The round vs. flat side shoots are the dead giveaway - just roll them between your fingers to feel the difference.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, clubmoss isn't actually a moss at all - it's more closely related to ferns! The "groundpine" name you might see in older books refers to its resemblance to tiny pine trees, and scientists have recently split what used to be one big confusing group into several distinct species.
compareHints: Prickly tree-clubmoss differs from flat-branched tree-clubmoss by having round (not flattened) side shoots and all leaves the same size, while flat-branched has different sized leaves. Compared to Hickey's tree-clubmoss, the prickly species has that distinctly rough, prickly texture and more densely packed uniform leaves that give it its characteristic bottle-brush feel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Flat-branched tree-clubmoss stands out from its relatives by its distinctly flattened, fan-like branching pattern - prickly tree-clubmoss has more rounded, bottle-brush-like branches, while Hickey's tree-clubmoss tends to be more upright and less flattened.
Hickey's tree-clubmoss differs from flat-branched tree-clubmoss by having more three-dimensional, upright branching rather than flattened, fan-like branches.
